title: The Voice in the Middle Row

passage.title: The Voice in the Middle Row
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
For three weeks, Elena had practiced the spring concert solo until her fingers knew every note on her violin neck. At home in her room, the high melody sounded bright and crisp. Yet each Tuesday in the school band room, the middle part felt flat. Elena tried bowing harder so her violin would ring above the rest of the group. Still, Ms. Ortiz tapped her stick on the stand and asked the strings to stop.

Instead of scolding the first violins, Ms. Ortiz asked Elena to trade seats with Malik in the middle row for ten minutes. Malik played the viola, an instrument slightly larger than a violin with a deeper, warmer voice. At first, Elena felt puzzled as she sat in the row and held her bow still. She had always thought the middle row just played soft chords while the front row kept the main tune.

When Ms. Ortiz raised her baton again, Elena listened from the center of the circle. Right away, she heard what her own loud playing had drowned out all month. The rich inner rhythm, carried across the slow measures by the warm wooden violas, was completely missed by Elena from her front-row chair. The violas were not playing dull filler notes at all. They were passing a steady, rising counter-melody that built a bridge between the deep cellos and her high violin line.

When Elena returned to her front seat, she stopped trying to overpower the room. Instead of rushing ahead on the high notes, she leaned her ear toward Malik's stand. She let her bow float on top of the viola chord. Her bright melody wove into their warm notes like silver thread through dark wool. The harsh edge vanished, and the whole string section sounded like one breathing instrument.

After the last chord faded, Ms. Ortiz smiled and lowered her stick without a single change. Malik gave Elena a glad nod from the middle row. Elena saw that leading a song did not mean playing the loudest part in the hall. True harmony happened only when she listened as carefully as she played.

tier2Words.definition: the main tune or sequence of musical notes in a song
tier2Words.contextClue: At home, the high main tune sounded bright and crisp on her violin.

tier2Words.definition: confused or unable to understand why something is happening
tier2Words.rootHint: Related to pose ('to put in a perplexed state')
tier2Words.contextClue: Elena did not understand why Ms. Ortiz asked her to sit in the middle row without playing.

tier2Words.definition: to be too loud or strong for others, drowning them out
tier2Words.rootHint: Prefix over- ('too much') + power ('strength or force')
tier2Words.contextClue: Instead of bowing harder to ring above the room, Elena softened her tone and leaned her ear toward Malik's stand.

tier2Words.definition: a pleasing blend of different musical notes played together as one
tier2Words.rootHint: Greek harmonia ('joining or agreement of sounds')
tier2Words.contextClue: When her bright violin wove into the warm viola notes, the whole string section sounded like one instrument.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"The rich inner rhythm, carried across the slow measures by the warm wooden violas, was completely missed by Elena from her front-row chair."

Based on the structure of the sentence, what played the inner rhythm, and who failed to hear it?

options.text: Elena carried the inner rhythm across the slow measures, and the wooden violas missed it.
options.childFeedback: This flips the two actions around! In Paragraph 3, the wooden violas carried the inner rhythm, while Elena was the one who missed hearing it.

options.text: The front-row chair carried the wooden violas across the band room while Elena watched.
options.childFeedback: A chair cannot carry instruments across a room! Paragraph 3 says Elena sat in her front-row chair while the warm wooden violas carried the rhythm.

options.text: The warm wooden violas carried the inner rhythm, and Elena missed it from her front-row chair.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, the first 'by' phrase shows that the warm wooden violas carried the inner rhythm, while 'missed by Elena' shows she failed to hear it from the front row.

options.text: Ms. Ortiz missed the spring concert because her wooden baton broke in half.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 never says Ms. Ortiz missed the concert or broke her baton; in Paragraph 1, she only tapped her stick to pause practice.

questions.provingSentenceText: The rich inner rhythm, carried across the slow measures by the warm wooden violas, was completely missed by Elena from her front-row chair.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, the first 'by' phrase shows that the warm wooden violas carried the inner rhythm, while 'missed by Elena' shows she failed to hear it from the front row.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive sentence, 'by the warm wooden violas' modifies 'carried' (what produced the rhythm), while 'was completely missed by Elena' identifies who failed to hear it.
questions.retryHint: Look closely at both 'by' phrases in Paragraph 3 to see what carried the rhythm and who missed it.

questions.prompt:
Read these sentences from Paragraph 4:

"When Elena returned to her front seat, she stopped trying to overpower the room. Instead of rushing ahead on the high notes, she leaned her ear toward Malik's stand."

What does the word overpower mean as it is used in Paragraph 4?

options.text: To play so loudly that one instrument drowns out the rest of the group
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, 'overpower' means to play so loudly that one instrument drowns out the rest of the group. Instead of bowing harder like in Paragraph 1, Elena softened her tone to blend in.

options.text: To whisper quietly so no one in the back row can hear the tune
options.childFeedback: Whispering quietly is the opposite of overpowering! Earlier, Elena bowed harder so her loud violin drowned out the middle row.

options.text: To plug electric amplifiers into the band room wall sockets
options.childFeedback: The school band room uses wooden string instruments, not electric amplifiers or wall sockets. 'Overpower' describes Elena playing too loudly with her bow.

options.text: To trade sheet music stands with a partner in the middle row
options.childFeedback: Elena traded seats with Malik in Paragraph 2, not sheet music stands in Paragraph 4. Here, 'overpower' means drowning out the other players with loud volume.

questions.provingSentenceText: When Elena returned to her front seat, she stopped trying to overpower the room.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, 'overpower' means to play so loudly that one instrument drowns out the rest of the group. Instead of bowing harder like in Paragraph 1, Elena softened her tone to blend in.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 1, Elena tried bowing harder to play louder than everyone else; in Paragraph 4, she stops trying to 'overpower' the room and instead blends her notes gently with the violas.
questions.retryHint: Compare Paragraph 1, where Elena bowed harder to ring above everyone, with Paragraph 4, where she lets her bow float gently.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 3, how does sitting in Malik's seat change Elena's view of the viola section?

options.text: She decides to quit playing the violin and switch to the cello before the spring concert.
options.childFeedback: Elena never quits the violin or switches to the cello! In Paragraph 4, she returns to her front-row violin seat after ten minutes.

options.text: She concludes that the middle row only plays quiet background filler chords.
options.childFeedback: That was what Elena used to think in Paragraph 2 before she listened! In Paragraph 3, she realizes the violas are not playing dull filler notes at all.

options.text: She realizes that Malik has been playing from the wrong sheet music for three weeks.
options.childFeedback: Malik is playing the right music the whole time. In Paragraph 3, Elena realizes her own loud violin had simply drowned out his steady viola part.

options.text: She discovers that the violas play a rising counter-melody that connects the deep cellos to her high violin part.
options.childFeedback: Sitting in Malik's seat lets Elena hear that the violas are not playing dull filler notes at all, but a rising counter-melody that connects the deep cellos to her high violin line.

questions.provingSentenceText: They were passing a steady, rising counter-melody that built a bridge between the deep cellos and her high violin line.
questions.childTip: Sitting in Malik's seat lets Elena hear that the violas are not playing dull filler notes at all, but a rising counter-melody that connects the deep cellos to her high violin line.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 3 (ELAGSE5RL3), sitting in Malik's seat shifts Elena's perspective from thinking violas play dull filler notes to hearing how their counter-melody bridges the cellos and violins.
questions.retryHint: Check the last two sentences of Paragraph 3 to see what Elena hears the violas playing instead of dull filler notes.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"Her bright melody wove into their warm notes like silver thread through dark wool."

Why does the author compare the violin and viola notes to silver thread and dark wool?

options.text: To explain that the students had to sew their own wool concert uniforms before Tuesday
options.childFeedback: No one is sewing concert clothes in Paragraph 4! 'Silver thread' and 'dark wool' are used as a comparison to describe how the high and low music notes blended.

options.text: To show how Elena's clear high notes and the violas' rich low notes blended together into one fabric of sound
options.childFeedback: Comparing Elena's high violin melody to bright silver thread and the deep viola notes to warm dark wool helps you picture how the two different sounds wove smoothly together.

options.text: To prove that violin strings are always made from spun sheep's wool
options.childFeedback: Violin strings are not made from sheep's wool. The author uses 'silver thread' and 'dark wool' to compare the bright violin sound with the warm viola sound.

options.text: To suggest that the music sounded scratchy and uncomfortable to the audience
options.childFeedback: Instead of sounding scratchy, the next sentence in Paragraph 4 says the harsh edge vanished and the strings sounded smooth and united.

questions.provingSentenceText: Her bright melody wove into their warm notes like silver thread through dark wool.
questions.childTip: Comparing Elena's high violin melody to bright silver thread and the deep viola notes to warm dark wool helps you picture how the two different sounds wove smoothly together.
questions.parentExplanation: The simile compares the high, bright violin tone ('silver thread') and the warm, deep viola tone ('dark wool') to show how the two contrasting sounds interlocked smoothly.
questions.retryHint: Picture bright silver thread weaving through warm dark wool in Paragraph 4: how do those two different textures fit together?

questions.prompt: Part A: How does Elena's approach to playing her solo change from the beginning of the passage to the end?

options.text: At first she wants Malik to play the solo, but by the end she insists on playing alone on stage.
options.childFeedback: Elena never asks Malik to take her solo, and at the end she blends her violin with the group instead of insisting on playing alone.

options.text: At first she refuses to practice at home, but by the end she practices for ten hours every night.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 says Elena had already practiced for three weeks at home until she knew every note, so refusing to practice wasn't her problem.

options.text: At first she tries to play louder than everyone else, but by the end she listens closely to blend her part with the other strings.
options.childFeedback: At the start in Paragraph 1, Elena bows harder to ring louder than everyone else, but by Paragraphs 4 and 5 she learns to listen closely so her violin blends with the group.

options.text: At first she plays the viola in the middle row, but by the end she switches to the cello.
options.childFeedback: Elena only sits in Malik's viola seat for ten minutes in Paragraph 2 to listen, and she never switches to playing the cello.

questions.provingSentenceText: True harmony happened only when she listened as carefully as she played.
questions.childTip: At the start in Paragraph 1, Elena bows harder to ring louder than everyone else, but by Paragraphs 4 and 5 she learns to listen closely so her violin blends with the group.
questions.parentExplanation: Tracking character change across the text (ELAGSE5RL3) shows Elena shifting from trying to ring above the room in Paragraph 1 to listening and blending in Paragraphs 4 and 5.
questions.retryHint: Compare how Elena tried to play in Paragraph 1 with what she learns about true harmony in Paragraph 5.
